498.title: Choose your company
498.hook: pick friends who are calm, since moods are catching (On Tranquility 7)
498.howItsDone: People who follow Seneca's advice pay attention to how the company they keep affects their mood, and seek out steady, calm friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: serve where you can, when the big stage is closed. Your line was serve where i can. Did the small private thing get done? Day four hundred ninety-eight.

Someone walks into the office in a foul mood, and within twenty minutes three other people are snapping too. Or the opposite: a friend who's simply easy to be around, and shoulders drop the moment they sit down. Nobody decided either thing. It just spread. Modern psychologists have a name for this: emotional contagion. Seneca didn't have the name, but he had the observation. In chapter seven of On Tranquility, after work and service, he turns to the people we spend our days with, and gives some very practical advice. Today: choose your company.
screen: `ONE FOUL MOOD, THREE SNAPPING.` → `ONE EASY FRIEND, SHOULDERS DROP.` → `IT SPREADS.`

segments.voice: First, the gift of a friend. Nothing, Seneca says, delights the mind like a faithful friendship: someone you can tell a secret to as safely as telling yourself, whose talk eases your worry and whose advice helps you decide. He's not cynical about people. He wants you to have friends. Second, choose with care. Vices spread, he warns, by contact. They pass to whoever is closest, the way an illness passes to those who sit by the sick bed. So pick, as far as you can, people who aren't ruled by their passions: not the rage-prone, not the greedy, not the one always in a panic. Third, don't wait for a saint. Seneca adds a realistic note. Don't go looking for a perfectly wise friend; people have searched for centuries. Choose the least bad. Steadiness, not perfection. Fourth, beware the moaner. The friend Seneca singles out is the one who's always gloomy, who complains about everything and finds a grievance in every piece of news. Even if they're loyal and kind, he says, a companion who's constantly upset is an enemy to your calm. Fair note: this isn't advice to abandon a friend who's grieving or ill. Seneca is talking about the mood we keep company with by habit, not the person who needs us right now. And it cuts both ways. If calm is catching, then so are you. Somebody is choosing your company too.
screen: `NOTHING DELIGHTS LIKE A FAITHFUL FRIEND.` · `VICES SPREAD BY CONTACT.` · `CHOOSE THE LEAST BAD.` · `BEWARE THE CONSTANT MOANER.` · then, large: `CALM IS CATCHING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the five people you spend the most time with, in person or on a screen. Picture each face for a breath. With each one, notice what your body does: does it settle, or tighten? No judging them. Just noticing. Now pick the one who settles you most. Picture sitting with them. Let some of their steadiness reach you now. Then ask: when people sit with me, what do they catch? The bell holds the time.
Choose your company. Seneca's advice in On Tranquility: moods and vices spread by contact, so keep close to the steady. Today's word.
Your line: calm is catching. Spend some time today with the steady person you pictured, even ten minutes or a call. And try to be someone worth catching. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

499.title: Less to lose
499.hook: Diogenes' slave ran away, and Diogenes let him go; fewer things, fewer wounds (On Tranquility 8)
499.howItsDone: People practicing Stoic simplicity sometimes give away possessions that cause more worry than use, aiming to be harder to wound rather than simply to own less.

segments.voice: Yesterday: choose your company, because moods spread by contact. Your line was calm is catching. Who did you sit with, and what did you catch? Day four hundred ninety-nine.

Have you ever bought something nice and then spent a week worrying about it? The new phone you're scared to drop. The car you check from the window. The white sofa no one is allowed to eat on. It was meant to make life easier, and it came with a small, permanent alarm attached. In chapter eight of On Tranquility, Seneca says that of all the things that trouble the mind, the biggest is money and what it buys. And he tells a story about the philosopher Diogenes, who, tradition says, lived in a large clay jar, on the day his only servant ran away. Today: less to lose.
screen: `THE WHITE SOFA NO ONE CAN SIT ON.` → `A SMALL, PERMANENT ALARM.` → `DIOGENES' SERVANT RUNS AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, Seneca's claim. People with little, he says, often suffer less than people with much, not because poverty is pleasant, but because they have less that can be taken. It hurts less, he observes, never to have had something than to lose it. Fortune has fewer places to strike. Second, the story. Diogenes owned one slave, named Manes. Manes ran away. Someone told Diogenes where he'd gone, and Diogenes didn't think it worth the trouble to bring him back. His reason: it would be shameful if Manes could live without Diogenes, and Diogenes couldn't live without Manes. Third, the honest flinch. The story treats a human being as a possession, as Seneca's whole world did. Diogenes is talking about a man as if he were a lost coat, and it's fair to flinch at that. But inside the story there's also something Diogenes may not have meant: Manes walked free, and Diogenes let him. Fourth, the point Seneca draws. He imagines Diogenes saying to Fortune: mind your own business, there's nothing of yours left here. Fewer things, fewer wounds. Seneca, who owned a great deal, isn't telling anyone to own nothing. He's asking which of your things own you. The phone you're afraid to drop. The status you'd hate to lose. Every one of them is a place where a bad day can reach in. Having less isn't the goal by itself. Being harder to wound is.
screen: `IT HURTS LESS NOT TO HAVE THAN TO LOSE.` · `MANES RAN; DIOGENES LET HIM GO.` · `THE HONEST FLINCH.` · `NOTHING OF FORTUNE'S LEFT HERE.` · then, large: `LESS TO LOSE.`

segments.voice: Look around you, or picture your home. Find one thing you own that you worry about more than you enjoy. Something that sets off a small alarm. Hold it in your mind. Imagine it gone: given away, sold, simply not there. Notice what happens in your chest. Relief? Panic? Both? If it's relief, you've found something you could let go. If it's panic, notice how much of you is tied to it. Either way, you know where the alarm is wired. The bell holds the time.
Less to lose. Diogenes let his runaway servant go, and Seneca draws the lesson: fewer things, fewer places for Fortune to wound. Today's word.
Your line: less to lose. Let one possession go this week: give it, sell it, donate it. Start with the one that sets off the alarm. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

500.title: Books to use
500.hook: books bought for show are furniture; buy what you'll read (On Tranquility 9)
500.howItsDone: Readers following Seneca sometimes read a few books deeply instead of collecting many, and choose books for use rather than display.

segments.voice: Yesterday: less to lose, Diogenes letting his runaway servant go. Your line was less to lose. Did you find the thing that sets off the alarm? Day five hundred.

Day five hundred. Five hundred mornings, or nights, or lunch breaks. Some of you missed plenty and came back, which counts. Now picture a bookshelf. Maybe yours. How many of those books have you actually read? And how many are there partly because of how they look: to a guest, on a video call, to the person you hoped to become when you bought them? No shame. Seneca's Rome had the same habit, at a much grander scale. In chapter nine of On Tranquility, right after money, he turns to the one expense that sounds above criticism. Books. Today: books to use.
screen: `DAY FIVE HUNDRED.` → `HOW MANY HAVE YOU READ?` → `THE EXPENSE ABOVE CRITICISM.`

segments.voice: First, even good spending has a limit. Spending on study, Seneca says, is the most honorable kind, but it's only reasonable within measure. What's the use of countless books and libraries whose owner can barely read the titles in a lifetime? A heap of books weighs on a learner; it doesn't teach. Better to give yourself to a few writers than to wander among many. Second, the great fire. Seneca brings up the library at Alexandria, where, he says, forty thousand books burned. The historian Livy had called that library a splendid monument to the taste and care of kings. Seneca disagrees, sharply. It wasn't taste and it wasn't care. It was studiosa luxuria, learned luxury. And then he takes even that back: not learned, since it was gathered for show, not for study. Third, books as furniture. He describes rich Romans who couldn't read well, whose dining rooms were lined with shelves to the ceiling, the book rolls valued for their handsome cases and labels. Among the baths and the fine furniture, Seneca says, a library had become one more thing a house was expected to have. Fourth, the point for us. Seneca isn't against books. He wrote shelves of them. He's against the gap between having and using, which by now you'll recognize: rich in enough, under the gold, mind the gap. A book you read twice is worth more to you than fifty you own.
screen: `EVEN STUDY SPENDING NEEDS MEASURE.` · `ALEXANDRIA: LEARNED LUXURY.` · `SHELVES TO THE DINING-ROOM CEILING.` · `HAVING VERSUS USING.` · then, large: `READ, DON'T DISPLAY.`

segments.voice: Picture your shelf, or your e-reader, or your saved articles. Let your eye travel along it. Find one book you bought for a real reason and never opened, or opened and set down. Remember why you wanted it. What were you hoping it would give you? Now picture actually opening it tonight: the first page, the chair, the light. Not to finish it. Just to use it, for twenty minutes, like a tool you finally picked up. The bell holds the time.
Books to use. Seneca's warning in On Tranquility: books gathered for show are furniture, even at Alexandria. Give yourself to a few, and read them. Today's word.
Your line: read, don't display. Take one shelf book down today and read twenty minutes of it. Day five hundred.

501.title: Minds need play
501.hook: Socrates played with children and Cato drank to relax; the mind needs rest (On Tranquility 17)
501.howItsDone: Readers of On Tranquility of Mind often build real rest and play into their week, treating it as part of keeping a steady mind rather than a break from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: books to use, Seneca on the library gathered for show. Your line was read, don't display. Which shelf book got its twenty minutes? Day five hundred one.

Seneca saves a surprise for the end of On Tranquility. After long stretches of hard advice about money, service, friends and books, he turns to Socrates, playing games with little children, and to Scipio, a celebrated Roman general, moving to music. All along he's been asking his friend Serenus to work at his calm. Now he writes something that sounds almost like a doctor's note from a Stoic: stop working at it for a while. Today: minds need play.
screen: `SOCRATES, PLAYING WITH CHILDREN.` → `A GENERAL, DANCING.` → `A DOCTOR'S NOTE FROM A STOIC.`

segments.voice: First, the bow. The mind, Seneca says, can't be held at the same tension all the time. It must be given rest; it will rise better and sharper for it. He compares it to a field: rich soil, cropped without a break, soon wears out. Constant work breeds a kind of dullness. Second, the examples. Socrates, Seneca says, wasn't ashamed to play with little boys. Cato, the stern senator, eased his mind with wine when public worries wore him down. Scipio, the general, would move to music, not in a soft way, Seneca adds quickly, but the way soldiers of old danced at festivals. Three famously serious men, one Greek and two Romans, and each had a way to put the seriousness down. Third, the honest note on wine. Seneca allows wine as one way to loosen the mind, and in moderation, he says, it can lift care. Plenty of people find rest without it, for reasons of faith, health or recovery, and nothing in his point depends on the cup. The point is release. Fourth, rest is part of the work. Lawgivers, Seneca says, fixed festival days, so that people would be made to rest. Some people need a nap at noon; some need a walk under the open sky. Tranquility isn't constant effort. It's knowing when to stop. Other paths keep something like it too: a Sabbath, a feast day, a day off. The mind that never plays isn't more serious. It's just more tired.
screen: `THE MIND CAN'T STAY AT FULL TENSION.` · `SOCRATES, CATO, SCIPIO AT REST.` · `WINE IS OPTIONAL; RELEASE IS NOT.` · `FESTIVAL DAYS, BY LAW.` · then, large: `MINDS NEED PLAY.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, let your mind off the leash. Don't meditate in the usual way. Remember the last time you played: a game, a silly song, building something with a child, kicking a ball, doodling in a meeting. Let the memory get vivid. Notice what your face did. Then let your mind wander wherever it wants, like a kid in a field. No goal, no lesson. If you smile, that counts. The bell holds the time.
Minds need play. Seneca's close to On Tranquility: Socrates played with children, Scipio danced, and the mind rises sharper after rest. Today's word.
Your line: minds need play. Play for ten minutes today, with no purpose. A game, a song, a ball, a child, a dog. Day five hundred one.

502.title: Canus at the board
502.hook: condemned by Caligula, Julius Canus finished his board game calmly (On Tranquility 14)
502.howItsDone: Readers of Seneca often remember Julius Canus when under pressure, finishing the task at hand calmly and fairly before reacting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: minds need play, Socrates on the floor with the children. Your line was minds need play. What did you play, and did your face remember how? Day five hundred two.

Rome, around the year 40. A man named Julius Canus has just finished a long argument with the emperor Caligula. As he turns to leave, Caligula tells him not to get his hopes up: he's already ordered his execution. Most people would beg, faint or run. Canus says: thank you, most excellent prince. Seneca admits he isn't sure what Canus meant. Was it irony, showing how cruel Caligula was if death came as a relief? Or real thanks? Either way, the next ten days are why On Tranquility remembers him. Today: Canus at the board.
screen: `CALIGULA: I'VE ORDERED YOUR DEATH.` → `THANK YOU, MOST EXCELLENT PRINCE.` → `TEN DAYS LEFT.`

segments.voice: First, the ten days. Roman custom then gave a condemned man ten days before execution. Seneca says Canus spent them without any sign of anxiety. Not hiding, not pleading, not bargaining. Living. Second, the board. When the centurion came for him, Canus was in the middle of a board game, a Roman strategy game played with little soldier pieces. He didn't jump up. He counted the pieces. Then he turned to his opponent and said: don't go claiming after I'm dead that you won. And he nodded to the centurion: you're my witness, I'm one piece ahead. Seneca asks: do you think Canus was only playing a game at that board? He was making a mockery of the tyrant. Third, the last question. His friends were weeping. Canus asked why they were sad. You're always arguing about whether the soul lives on, he said; I'm about to find out. He told them he meant to watch closely, in that last moment, to see whether the mind could feel itself leaving, and if he learned anything he'd come back and tell them. The sources are silent on what happened next. Fourth, what we take from it. Not that death is nothing, or that we should be cheerful facing cruelty. Canus was under a tyrant's sentence, and the story is a loss as well as an example. What stays is the board. Under the worst pressure there is, he finished what was in front of him, honestly, and kept score fairly. That's something an ordinary deadline can borrow.
screen: `TEN DAYS WITHOUT ANXIETY.` · `I'M ONE PIECE AHEAD.` · `I'M ABOUT TO FIND OUT.` · `FINISH WHAT'S IN FRONT OF YOU.` · then, large: `FINISH THE GAME.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're in the middle of that pressure keeps tempting you to abandon or rush. A task, a conversation, a piece of work. Picture the pressure arriving like a knock at the door. Now picture yourself not jumping up. You look at the board. You count the pieces: what's done, what's left. You make the next fair move. Breathe slowly while you picture it. Calm isn't the absence of the knock. It's finishing the move. The bell holds the time.
Canus at the board. Condemned by Caligula, he spent ten days calmly, and when the centurion came, he counted the pieces and finished the game. Today's word.
Your line: finish the game. When pressure hits today, finish one thing calmly before you react. Count the pieces first. Day five hundred two.

503.title: Brief madness
503.hook: anger is a brief madness, Seneca begins his book on it (On Anger 1.1)
503.howItsDone: Readers of Seneca's On Anger often learn their own first bodily signs of anger and name them as they happen, to catch anger before it speaks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Canus at the board, counting the pieces as the centurion waited. Your line was finish the game. Did you finish one thing before reacting? Day five hundred three.
screen: `CANUS AT THE BOARD — FINISH THE GAME.`

segments.voice: Anger has a face, and the angry person almost never sees it. Everyone else does. Seneca's brother Novatus once asked him to write about how anger might be calmed. Seneca answered at length, and he opens not with a definition but with a mirror. Of all the passions, he says, anger is the most hideous and the most frenzied. Then he borrows a short name for it from wise men who came before him. Today: brief madness.
screen: `ANGER HAS A FACE.` → `A BROTHER ASKS FOR HELP.` → `HE OPENS WITH A MIRROR.`

segments.voice: First, the phrase. Some wise men, Seneca writes, have called anger a brief madness. In Latin, brevis insania. Like madness, it forgets decency, ignores friendship, won't listen to reason, and charges at what it wants even when the charge will hurt itself. The only difference is that it passes. Usually. Second, the mirror. Seneca describes the angry face in close-up, and it's not flattering: eyes blazing, face flushing as the blood rushes up, lips trembling, teeth clenched, breath hissing, hands clapping together, feet stamping. You can't tell, he says, whether this vice is more hateful or more ugly. He wants Novatus to see what everyone else sees. Third, the body knows first. Notice that Seneca's list is all body. Long before we decide we're angry, the jaw has tightened, the heat has risen, the voice has gotten louder. Those are the first signs, and they're the useful ones, because they show up while there's still a gap before the words come out. Fourth, why this matters now. Seneca will spend the rest of the work on what to do about anger. But the start is simply recognizing it. You can't step out of a madness you don't notice you're in. A short madness is still a madness: a texted reply, a slammed door, a sentence you can't take back, all before the heat has even cooled. Naming it as madness, while it's happening, is Seneca's first step.
screen: `SOME WISE MEN: A BRIEF MADNESS.` · `THE ANGRY FACE, IN CLOSE-UP.` · `THE BODY KNOWS FIRST.` · `NAME IT WHILE IT'S HAPPENING.` · then, large: `BRIEF MADNESS.`

segments.voice: Bring back a recent moment of anger, a small one. Replay it slowly, but don't follow the story. Follow your body. Where did it start? A hot face, a tight jaw, a quick breath, fists, a jump in your voice? Find your first sign: the one that shows up before anything else. Now breathe out slowly and let that part of your body soften. Remember where it is. That's your early-warning bell. The bell holds the time.
Brief madness. Seneca's opening to On Anger: some wise men called anger a brief madness, deaf to reason, ugly in the face. Today's word.
Your line: brief madness. Today, the first time you feel your early-warning sign, name it quietly: brief madness. That's all. Just the name. Day five hundred three.

504.title: Delay is the cure
504.hook: the best cure for anger is delay (On Anger 2.29)
504.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca set a rule to wait before acting or replying in anger, sometimes an hour, sometimes a night, to let the first rush pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday: brief madness, anger in the mirror. Your line was brief madness. Where did your early-warning sign show up, and did you name it? Day five hundred four, the end of a week.

The email arrives at 4:52 on a Friday. It's unfair, it's wrong, and it copies your boss. Your fingers are already typing. The reply is excellent. It's sharp, it's true, it would feel wonderful to send. Replies like that get written every day. Some get sent. Yesterday Seneca named anger: a brief madness. Today, deep in his second book, he gives what he calls the greatest remedy for it, and it's almost disappointingly simple. Not a technique. Not a philosophy. Just time. Today: delay is the cure.
screen: `4:52 ON A FRIDAY.` → `THE REPLY IS EXCELLENT.` → `SENECA'S GREATEST REMEDY: TIME.`

segments.voice: First, the line. The greatest remedy for anger, Seneca says, is delay. Ask anger for time, not so that it will forgive, but so that it can judge. Its first rush is heavy; if it waits, it eases. You don't have to win the argument with anger. You just have to outlast its first wave. Second, don't try to remove it all at once. Seneca is realistic. Trying to rip anger out by force, in the first moment, rarely works. Picking it apart a little at a time does. Wait, and the parts loosen. Third, while you wait, judge. Seneca says much of our anger rests on things we believed too quickly: a rumor, a look, a tone of voice in a message. Delay gives you time to ask the other side, to check the facts, to wonder whether there's a story you don't know. An angry reply can collapse under one question. Fourth, a teacher we've met. Remember Athenodorus, who advised serving where you can? Possibly the same man; some readers think so. The later writer Plutarch says that when Athenodorus left the court of the emperor Augustus, his parting advice was: when you're angry, don't say or do anything until you've recited the alphabet to yourself. Twenty-four Greek letters. That's a delay you can carry anywhere. And our week, looking back: calm is catching, less to lose, read, don't display, minds need play, finish the game, brief madness. Seneca's tools are rarely dramatic. A friend, a plain shelf, a game, a breath, and now, a pause.
screen: `THE GREATEST REMEDY IS DELAY.` · `NOT ALL AT ONCE.` · `WAIT, THEN JUDGE.` · `ATHENODORUS: RECITE THE ALPHABET.` · then, large: `DELAY.`

segments.voice: Think of a reply you're tempted to send, or a conversation you're tempted to have, while you're still hot. Picture writing it. Now picture not sending it. Put it in a drawer, a draft folder, an envelope. Notice what the waiting is like. Itchy? Unfinished? A little relieved? Breathe through it. While you breathe, ask one question you skipped: what might I not know about this? The bell holds the time.
Delay is the cure. Seneca's greatest remedy for anger: give it time, not to forgive, but to judge. Its first rush passes. Today's word.
Your line: delay. The next time a reply comes hot, wait one hour before you send it. If an hour is impossible, recite the alphabet first. Day five hundred four.

fork.setup: an unfair email arrives on Friday afternoon, copying your boss. your reply is ready. what does Seneca's remedy say?
options: wait; let the first rush pass, then judge.
fork.reveal: delay, he says, is the greatest remedy: anger's first wave is heavy and passes if it waits.

original.note: Latin, 'delay': Seneca's greatest remedy for anger.

trapdoor: what you thought: delay means suppressing your anger.
what it means: delay gives anger time to judge; its first rush passes, and facts can be checked.
what a scholar hears: Seneca gives the delay remedy more than once in On Anger (at 2.29 and again at 3.12); the alphabet story comes from Plutarch's Sayings of Romans, not from Seneca.
